title: Fashion & Style
subtitle: Talk style, dress for the occasion, and debate the true cost of fast fashion

lessons.title: La mode française
lessons.description: Describe an outfit and a personal style with precision — cut, fabric, prints, and the vocabulary French speakers use to talk fashion.

blocks.heading: Describing a look: coupe, matière, imprimé
blocks.body: To describe an outfit like a French speaker, go beyond colour and name. La coupe is the cut — how the garment is shaped and falls on the body. La matière is what it's made of, and l'imprimé is any printed pattern. Combine them with en (material) and à (pattern) to build a full description in one sentence.

examples.french: J'aime la coupe ample de cette veste.
examples.english: I like the loose cut of this jacket.

examples.french: C'est en quelle matière, ce chemisier ?
examples.english: What's this blouse made of?

examples.french: Elle porte une jupe à imprimé fleuri.
examples.english: She's wearing a skirt with a floral print.

examples.french: J'ai trouvé une chemise à rayures fines.
examples.english: I found a shirt with thin stripes.

examples.french: Il préfère les tee-shirts unis aux tee-shirts à motifs.
examples.english: He prefers plain T-shirts to patterned ones.

examples.french: Cette robe à pois me rappelle les années cinquante.
examples.english: This polka-dot dress reminds me of the fifties.

blocks.tip: Uni means "plain, solid-coloured" here — a completely different word from une université. Context makes it obvious.

blocks.heading: Naming a style: du sobre à l'extravagant
blocks.body: French has a rich scale of adjectives for personal style, from sobre (understated) through chic and élégant to sophistiqué, minimaliste, or, at the other end, excentrique and extravagant. Avoir du style means "to have a good eye for putting an outfit together" — it's a compliment independent of following trends.

examples.french: Son style est très sobre : noir, blanc, jamais d'imprimé.
examples.english: Her style is very understated: black, white, never any print.

examples.french: Elle a toujours eu du style, même étudiante.

examples.english: He has a slightly eccentric style, but it suits him.

examples.french: Sa robe était sophistiquée sans être trop habillée.
examples.english: Her dress was sophisticated without being too dressy.

blocks.tip: Branché is the informal word for "trendy, in the know" — useful when talking about people, not just clothes: "Elle est très branchée."

blocks.heading: The people and words behind the industry
blocks.body: Le couturier / la couturière designs haute couture: unique, hand-made pieces. Le styliste / la styliste designs for prêt-à-porter, ready-to-wear collections sold in shops. Le mannequin (always masculine, even for a woman) presents the collection at a défilé. Une collection groups everything a brand shows for one season.

examples.french: Ce couturier ne présente qu'une collection de haute couture par an.
examples.english: This couturier only presents one haute couture collection a year.

examples.french: La styliste a lancé sa propre marque à vingt-cinq ans.

examples.french: Le mannequin portait une robe entièrement brodée.

examples.french: Le défilé a duré à peine quinze minutes.

examples.french: Le prêt-à-porter coûte bien moins cher que la haute couture.

examples.french: Cette collection s'inspire des années quatre-vingt.
examples.english: This collection is inspired by the eighties.

blocks.tip: Paris Fashion Week is called la Fashion Week de Paris in everyday French — the English term is used even in French headlines.

blocks.heading: Relative pronouns qui, que, dont — describing precisely
blocks.body: To describe clothes without endless short sentences, French uses relative pronouns. Qui replaces the subject of the next clause; que replaces the object; dont replaces de + noun (talking about, made of, needing). Choosing the right one is a classic B1 hurdle, but the logic is simple: look at the verb right after the pronoun.

examples.french: J'aime la veste qui est dans la vitrine.
examples.english: I like the jacket that's in the window.

examples.french: C'est la robe que j'ai portée à son mariage.
examples.english: It's the dress I wore to her wedding.

examples.french: Le styliste dont on parle beaucoup vient d'ouvrir sa boutique.
examples.english: The stylist everyone is talking about has just opened his shop.

examples.french: La marque dont elle est fan propose enfin du prêt-à-porter durable.
examples.english: The brand she's a fan of is finally offering sustainable ready-to-wear.

blocks.tip: If the next word is a conjugated verb, try qui first. If a subject and verb already follow, it's que or dont.

blocks.heading: Demonstrative pronouns celui, celle, ceux, celles — comparing looks
blocks.body: When comparing outfits without repeating the noun, use celui (m. sg.), celle (f. sg.), ceux (m. pl.), celles (f. pl.). They never stand alone: follow them with -ci / -là, de + noun, or a relative clause (qui/que/dont).

examples.french: J'aime cette veste, mais je préfère celle-ci.
examples.english: I like that jacket, but I prefer this one.

blocks.tip: Never say "celui de la robe qui" — pick one link at a time: celle de + noun, OR celle qui/que/dont, never both.

passages.title: Le style de Camille
passages.french:
Camille travaille dans une boutique de prêt-à-porter à Lyon, et son propre style intrigue tout le monde.
Elle ne suit jamais vraiment les tendances ; elle préfère les pièces qui traversent les saisons sans se démoder.
« Ma garde-robe est presque toute unie, dit-elle. Le noir, le blanc, un peu de bleu marine. »
Pourtant, son look n'a rien d'ennuyeux : elle joue sur la coupe, la matière et les accessoires.
Un imprimé, elle en porte un seul à la fois, jamais deux en même temps.
« C'est la règle que je me suis fixée », explique-t-elle en riant.
Ses bijoux viennent souvent de créateurs indépendants, ceux qu'elle découvre sur les marchés.
« Je préfère une pièce unique à un sac de marque que tout le monde a déjà. »
Camille reconnaît qu'elle a mis des années à trouver ce style sobre et personnel.
Avant, elle achetait tout ce qui était à la mode, sans se demander si ça lui allait vraiment.
Aujourd'hui, elle conseille ses clientes avec la même philosophie : mieux vaut avoir du style que suivre la mode.
« Le look que je préfère, ce n'est jamais celui du magazine. C'est celui qui te ressemble. »
passages.english:
Camille works in a ready-to-wear shop in Lyon, and her own style intrigues everyone.
She never really follows trends; she prefers pieces that last through the seasons without going out of style.
"My wardrobe is almost entirely plain," she says. "Black, white, a bit of navy blue."
And yet her look is anything but boring: she plays with cut, fabric and accessories.
She wears one print at a time, never two at once.
"It's the rule I've set myself," she explains, laughing.
Her jewellery often comes from independent designers, the ones she discovers at markets.
"I'd rather have a unique piece than a brand-name bag that everyone already owns."
Camille admits it took her years to find this understated, personal style.
Before, she used to buy whatever was fashionable, without wondering if it really suited her.
Today she advises her customers with the same philosophy: it's better to have style than to follow fashion.
"The look I prefer is never the one in the magazine. It's the one that looks like you."

lessons.title: S'habiller pour l'occasion
lessons.description: Read a dress code, dress appropriately for formal, casual, and in-between occasions, and talk about what's expected — or judged — in each setting.

blocks.heading: Le code vestimentaire : ce qui est exigé, toléré, interdit
blocks.body: Le code vestimentaire is the dress code — written or unwritten — for a place or an event. Something can be de rigueur (compulsory by convention), exigé (formally required), toléré (allowed, though not ideal), or simply déplacé (out of place). Respecter le code vestimentaire is the standard phrase for following it.

examples.french: La cravate est de rigueur dans ce restaurant.
examples.english: A tie is required at this restaurant.

examples.french: Le code vestimentaire de l'entreprise reste assez strict.
examples.english: The company's dress code remains fairly strict.

examples.french: Un jean est toléré le vendredi, mais pas devant les clients.
examples.english: Jeans are tolerated on Fridays, but not in front of clients.

examples.french: Une tenue de sport serait déplacée à ce mariage.
examples.english: Sportswear would be out of place at this wedding.

examples.french: On nous a demandé de respecter un code vestimentaire précis.
examples.english: We were asked to respect a specific dress code.

examples.french: Le short n'est pas exigé, mais fortement conseillé pour ce cours.
examples.english: Shorts aren't required, but strongly recommended for this class.

blocks.tip: De rigueur always follows the noun it describes and stays invariable: la cravate est de rigueur, les cravates sont de rigueur.

blocks.heading: Du décontracté au strict
blocks.body: French distinguishes several degrees of formality: décontracté (relaxed, casual), habillé (dressed up, smart), soigné (neat, well turned out — a compliment about care, not formality), négligé (careless, sloppy), and strict (severe, formal without warmth). Convenable simply means "appropriate for the situation", regardless of how formal that situation is.

examples.french: C'est une soirée décontractée, viens comme tu es.
examples.english: It's a casual evening, come as you are.

examples.french: Il était très habillé pour un simple déjeuner entre amis.
examples.english: He was very dressed up for a simple lunch with friends.

examples.french: Elle est toujours soignée, même en jean et tee-shirt.
examples.english: She's always neat, even in jeans and a T-shirt.

examples.french: Sa tenue négligée a surpris tout le monde à l'entretien.
examples.english: His sloppy outfit surprised everyone at the interview.

examples.french: Le costume est trop strict pour ce genre de soirée.
examples.english: The suit is too formal for this kind of party.

examples.french: Une chemise et un pantalon, c'est tout à fait convenable.
examples.english: A shirt and trousers, that's completely appropriate.

blocks.tip: Habillé alone often just means "dressed" (je suis habillé, I'm dressed), but with très or trop it shifts to "dressed up, formal".

blocks.heading: S'adapter sans se tromper
blocks.body: Choosing what to wear is also about reading a social situation: s'adapter au contexte, faire attention aux convenances (the social proprieties), and avoiding détonner — clashing or standing out for the wrong reason. Une tenue qui correspond à l'occasion sends the right signal; the wrong one can donner le mauvais ton or ruin a première impression.

examples.french: Il faut savoir s'adapter selon le lieu et les gens qu'on va rencontrer.
examples.english: You need to know how to adapt depending on the place and the people you'll meet.

examples.french: Sa tenue ne correspondait pas du tout à l'ambiance de la soirée.
examples.english: His outfit didn't match the mood of the evening at all.

examples.french: Mieux vaut respecter les convenances la première fois qu'on est invité.
examples.english: It's better to respect the social conventions the first time you're invited.

examples.french: Avec ce costume trop voyant, il détonnait complètement.
examples.english: With that overly flashy suit, he clashed completely.

examples.french: On dit souvent que la tenue donne le ton d'une soirée.
examples.english: People often say the outfit sets the tone of an evening.

examples.french: Une bonne tenue peut vraiment impressionner un recruteur.
examples.english: A good outfit can really impress a recruiter.

blocks.tip: In job-interview contexts, French speakers often reuse le registre (register) from language to talk about clothes: un registre plus formel.

blocks.heading: The subjunctive after obligation and necessity
blocks.body: Dress codes are full of obligation, and French marks it with the subjunctive after expressions like il faut que, il est important que, il vaut mieux que, and il est essentiel que. The subjunctive shows the outcome is required or desired, not a fact. Regular -er verbs follow the same base as the present tense nous form.

blocks.heading: Comparing formality: plus... que, le plus... de
blocks.body: To compare how dressy an outfit or event is, use plus/moins/aussi + adjective + que for two things, and le/la/les plus + adjective + de for a superlative within a group. Bon and bien have irregular comparatives: meilleur(e) and mieux.

passages.title: Une semaine, quatre tenues
passages.french:
Léa a eu une semaine chargée, avec quatre occasions bien différentes à habiller.
Lundi, entretien d'embauche : elle a choisi un tailleur gris, sobre et bien coupé.
« Je voulais rester dans un registre formel sans paraître trop strict », explique-t-elle.
Mercredi soir, vernissage d'une amie artiste : là, le code était plutôt chic décontracté.
Elle a opté pour une robe unie et des bijoux discrets, rien qui ne détonne dans une galerie.
Vendredi, réunion d'équipe informelle : jean et chemise, comme tout le monde au bureau ce jour-là.
« Le vendredi, personne ne juge personne sur la tenue », dit-elle en riant.
Samedi enfin, le mariage d'un cousin, où la consigne était claire : tenue de soirée exigée.
Léa a sorti une robe qu'elle garde justement pour ces occasions-là.
« Il faut que je sois élégante, sans voler la vedette à la mariée », plaisante-t-elle.
Ce qui l'a le plus surprise cette semaine, c'est à quel point s'adapter est devenu naturel.
« Avant, je me trompais souvent. Maintenant, je sais lire un code vestimentaire d'un coup d'œil. »
passages.english:
Léa had a busy week, with four very different occasions to dress for.
Monday, job interview: she chose a grey suit, understated and well cut.
"I wanted to stay in a formal register without looking too severe," she explains.
Wednesday evening, a friend's art opening: there, the code was more smart-casual.
She went for a plain dress and discreet jewellery, nothing that would clash in a gallery.
Friday, an informal team meeting: jeans and a shirt, like everyone else at the office that day.
"On Fridays, nobody judges anybody on their outfit," she says, laughing.
Saturday, finally, a cousin's wedding, where the instruction was clear: evening wear required.
Léa took out a dress she keeps specifically for occasions like that.
"I need to look elegant, without stealing the bride's spotlight," she jokes.
What surprised her most this week was how natural adapting has become.
"Before, I often got it wrong. Now I can read a dress code at a glance."

lessons.title: La fast fashion
lessons.description: Debate fast fashion versus sustainable consumption with balanced arguments, connectors, and the vocabulary to weigh cost, ethics, and the environment.

blocks.heading: Qu'est-ce que la fast fashion ?
blocks.body: La fast fashion — the English term is used directly in French — describes clothes produced very quickly and cheaply, meant to be worn briefly and often jetés (thrown away) rather than reused. L'industrie textile is criticised for la surproduction, la pollution it generates, and les conditions de travail of the travailleurs and travailleuses who make the clothes, sometimes sous-payés.

examples.french: La fast fashion produit des vêtements presque jetables.
examples.english: Fast fashion produces almost disposable clothes.

examples.french: L'industrie textile est l'une des plus polluantes au monde.
examples.english: The textile industry is one of the most polluting in the world.

examples.french: La surproduction pousse les marques à baisser sans cesse les prix.
examples.english: Overproduction pushes brands to keep lowering prices.

examples.french: Beaucoup de travailleurs du textile sont sous-payés.
examples.english: Many textile workers are underpaid.

examples.french: Les conditions de travail dans certaines usines restent inquiétantes.
examples.english: Working conditions in some factories remain worrying.

examples.french: Un tee-shirt à cinq euros a forcément un coût caché.
examples.english: A five-euro T-shirt necessarily has a hidden cost.

blocks.tip: Éphémère (short-lived) is a useful word here: la mode éphémère describes trends designed to be outdated within weeks.

blocks.heading: Les alternatives : slow fashion, seconde main, recyclage
blocks.body: In response, more people privilégient (favour) la slow fashion and une consommation plus durable: buying d'occasion, in a friperie, or from brands offering une meilleure traçabilité and une fabrication locale. Le surcyclage (upcycling) transforms an old garment into something new instead of jeter and racheter.

examples.french: Je privilégie la seconde main pour la plupart de mes achats.
examples.english: I favour second-hand for most of my purchases.

examples.french: Cette friperie propose des pièces des années quatre-vingt.
examples.english: This second-hand shop offers pieces from the eighties.

examples.french: La marque garantit une meilleure traçabilité de ses tissus.
examples.english: The brand guarantees better traceability of its fabrics.

examples.french: Le surcyclage donne une seconde vie aux vêtements abîmés.
examples.english: Upcycling gives damaged clothes a second life.

examples.french: La fabrication locale coûte plus cher, mais dure plus longtemps.
examples.english: Local manufacturing costs more, but lasts longer.

examples.french: La durabilité d'un vêtement compte plus que son prix pour moi.
examples.english: A garment's durability matters more than its price to me.

blocks.tip: La slow fashion is not a French phrase but borrowed whole, exactly like la fast fashion — both stay invariable and untranslated in everyday speech.

blocks.heading: Débattre avec nuance
blocks.body: A balanced debate needs phrases that concede a point before qualifying it. D'un côté... de l'autre côté sets up two sides; certes... mais admits something is true before contradicting it; il ne faut pas culpabiliser reminds people not to feel guilty for imperfect choices, while prendre conscience de means becoming aware of an issue.

examples.french: D'un côté, la fast fashion rend la mode accessible à tous.
examples.english: On one hand, fast fashion makes fashion accessible to everyone.

examples.french: De l'autre côté, elle encourage une consommation excessive.
examples.english: On the other hand, it encourages excessive consumption.

examples.french: Certes, tout le monde n'a pas les moyens de payer plus cher, mais il existe des solutions.
examples.english: Granted, not everyone can afford to pay more, but solutions exist.

examples.french: Il ne faut pas culpabiliser ceux qui achètent en fonction de leur budget.
examples.english: We shouldn't make people who buy according to their budget feel guilty.

examples.french: Beaucoup de gens ont pris conscience de l'impact de leurs achats.
examples.english: Many people have become aware of the impact of their purchases.

examples.french: Boycotter une marque ne change pas tout, mais ça envoie un message.
examples.english: Boycotting a brand doesn't change everything, but it sends a message.

blocks.tip: Sensibiliser (to raise awareness) is the verb French debates use constantly: sensibiliser le public, sensibiliser les jeunes.

blocks.heading: Giving an opinion: indicative or subjunctive?
blocks.body: Verbs like penser, croire, and trouver take the indicative when affirmative (je pense que + fact), but switch to the subjunctive when negated, because the statement becomes uncertain: je ne pense pas que + subjunctive. Verbs that inherently express doubt, wish, or judgement — douter que, vouloir que, il est dommage que — always take the subjunctive.

examples.english: I think fast fashion is a real ecological problem.

examples.english: I don't think that's the only solution.

examples.english: We want brands to be more transparent.

blocks.tip: Croire and penser only trigger the subjunctive when negated or in a question expressing real doubt — not automatically.

blocks.heading: Structuring an argument: cause and consequence
blocks.body: A good debate links ideas clearly. Car and puisque introduce a reason (puisque often signals shared knowledge), while donc and c'est pourquoi introduce a consequence. Grâce à points to a positive cause, à cause de a negative one. These connectors turn a list of facts into a real argument.

examples.english: Because of overproduction, some clothes are never even sold.

blocks.tip: Grâce à and à cause de are never interchangeable: grâce à is always positive, à cause de is always negative or neutral-negative.

passages.title: Fast fashion : faut-il culpabiliser ?
passages.french:
La fast fashion divise, et le débat mérite d'être nuancé plutôt que tranché en deux minutes.
D'un côté, elle a rendu la mode accessible : on peut aujourd'hui s'habiller pour presque rien.
Pour beaucoup de familles, ce n'est pas un choix éthique, c'est simplement une question de budget.
De l'autre côté, cette accessibilité a un coût qu'on ne voit pas sur l'étiquette.
L'industrie textile figure parmi les plus polluantes au monde, et les conditions de travail restent souvent inquiétantes.
Certes, quelques marques communiquent sur leur traçabilité, mais l'information reste difficile à vérifier.
Puisque le consommateur ne peut pas tout contrôler, faut-il vraiment le culpabiliser à chaque achat ?
Beaucoup de spécialistes pensent que non : mieux vaut sensibiliser que faire honte.
Prendre conscience de l'impact de ses achats, ce n'est pas la même chose que tout changer du jour au lendemain.
Certains privilégient déjà la friperie, le surcyclage ou la fabrication locale, quand leur budget le permet.
D'autres commencent simplement par garder leurs vêtements plus longtemps, ce qui est déjà un premier pas.
Le vrai changement viendra sans doute autant des marques que des habitudes de chacun.
passages.english:
Fast fashion divides opinion, and the debate deserves nuance rather than a two-minute verdict.
On one hand, it has made fashion accessible: today you can get dressed for almost nothing.
For many families, it isn't an ethical choice, it's simply a matter of budget.
On the other hand, that accessibility has a cost you don't see on the price tag.
The textile industry is among the most polluting in the world, and working conditions often remain worrying.
Granted, a few brands communicate about their traceability, but the information stays hard to verify.
Since the consumer can't control everything, should we really make them feel guilty for every purchase?
Many experts think not: it's better to raise awareness than to shame people.
Becoming aware of the impact of your purchases isn't the same thing as changing everything overnight.
Some people already favour second-hand shops, upcycling, or local manufacturing, when their budget allows it.
Others simply start by keeping their clothes longer, which is already a first step.
Real change will probably come as much from brands as from everyone's habits.
